text: Ensembles with different structures. <break time="0.8s" /> May encounter different group dynamics. <break time="0.8s" /> For instance. <break time="0.8s" /> Ford and Davidson studied members of 20 professional and semi professional wind quintets. <break time="0.8s" /> In the United Kingdom. <break time="0.8s" /> The technique and timbres of the instruments of the wind quintet. <break time="0.8s" /> Which typically comprises a flute, oboe, clarinet, French horn, and bassoon. <break time="0.8s" /> Are more distinct than those of string quartets. <break time="0.8s" /> And intragroup dynamics may be quite different from quartets. <break time="0.8s" /> Due to the odd number of members. <break time="0.8s" /> Dynamics inherent in the way the music is scored. <break time="0.8s" /> Afford greater opportunities for democracy within the group. <break time="0.8s" /> Such as more equality and interchangeability among musical parts. <break time="0.8s" /> For example, the flute is often assigned the melody. <break time="0.8s" /> But sometimes also plays an inner part. <break time="0.8s" /> Unlike the more rigid string quartet. <break time="0.8s" /> There is also more flexibility. <break time="0.8s" /> In seating arrangements for wind quintets. <break time="0.8s" /> In addition although the flute player was most frequently named as the leader. <break time="0.8s" /> Members of wind quintets were less likely. <break time="0.8s" /> To identify a clear leader. <break time="0.8s" /> Than members of string quartets. <break time="0.8s" /> In Murnighan and Conlons study. <break time="0.8s" /> Instead Ford and Davidson noted. <break time="0.8s" /> That in most of the quintets. <break time="0.8s" /> Players took equal responsibility for leading the ensemble. <break time="0.8s" /> The musical structure and social structure of the group. <break time="0.8s" /> Seem to reflect each other.
